tips.title: She performs it, she did not write it
tips.body: The set work is listed under **Esperanza Spalding**, so it is easy to call her the composer. **Baden Powell** composed the music and **Vinicius de Moraes** wrote the Portuguese words. Spalding sings and plays the bass.

tips.title: Complex harmony is not modulation
tips.body: Extensions, a diminished seventh, chromatic chords and a chromatic descending bass — and the piece still **never leaves B minor**. Underneath, the chord roots move around **I, II, IV and V**.

tips.title: Bar 19 doubles twice over
tips.body: The tempo almost doubles, and the **note values double too**. So verse 2's phrases only *look* longer than verse 1's — the two changes cancel. The guide calls the apparent increase **false**.

tips.title: A leaps, B steps
tips.body: Melody A moves mostly by **leap**, melody B almost entirely by **step**. Remember it as the contrast that lets you tell the two apart when they are combined at bars 89 to 104.

tips.title: Bars 89 to 104 answer three questions
tips.body: Structural climax (the two melodies together), textural climax (the only **polyphony**), and a rhythmic point (verse 2's rhythms become less syncopated, perhaps so they fit). One passage, three points.

why.matters: Bossa nova is a fusion that stopped sounding like one: Brazilian samba crossed with American jazz, and *bossa nova* means new trend. This set work has three performing forces only, and one performer sings and plays the bass at the same time; it has harmony complicated enough to sound as if it must be going somewhere, and a key that never moves; and it has three people to credit, the performer, the composer and the lyricist, which is an easy mark to lose. It is here to show how much a fusion can do with almost nothing.

examples.title: Three names on one track
examples.body: The set work is listed under Esperanza Spalding's name, and she did not write it. Baden Powell composed it, Vinicius de Moraes wrote the Portuguese words, and Spalding sings it and plays the bass. A question that asks who the composer is expects *Powell*, and *Spalding* scores nothing. The lesson generalises: a performer's name on a track is not a composer's, and a listening exam can test whether you know the difference.

examples.title: The harmony that goes nowhere
examples.body: Sevenths, ninths, elevenths and thirteenths piled on the triads, a diminished seventh, chromatic chords with notes from outside the key, a bass that slides down by semitone: it sounds as though the music must be modulating. It never does. It stays in B minor from the first bar to the last, and the roots underneath all that colour still move round chords I, II, IV and V, the same foundations as much simpler music. Hearing past the surface to the ordinary skeleton is the observation that earns.

steps.title: Where this sits, and who wrote it
steps.body:
This is a set work for **Area of Study 4: Fusions**, alongside Afro Celt Sound System's *Release*. A **fusion** is music that brings together two or more distinct styles or traditions.

**The fusion here is bossa nova**: Brazilian **samba** crossed with American **jazz**. *Bossa nova* means **new trend**, and it was one of the most popular styles of the late 1950s and early 1960s.

**Three people, and all three are worth knowing.** The set work is listed under Esperanza Spalding's name, so it is very easy to call her the composer. She is not.

- **Esperanza Spalding** — the **performer**. Born in Portland, Oregon in 1984, she moved from violin to double bass and studied at Berklee. She has won four Grammy awards, including Best New Artist in 2011. On this track she **sings and plays the bass at the same time**.
- **Baden Powell** (1937 to 2000) — the **composer**. A Brazilian guitarist who was central to the bossa nova explosion of the 1960s, mixing Brazilian rhythms with complex jazz harmonies.
- **Vinicius de Moraes** (1913 to 1980) — the **lyricist**. A poet and a career diplomat, who wrote the Oscar-winning film *Black Orpheus* and the words to *The Girl from Ipanema*.

The song was written in **1962**; Spalding recorded it on her album *Esperanza* in 2008. The words are in **Portuguese**, and they are about loss: *without you, my love, I am no one*. The Portuguese word **saudade** in verse 2 has no single English word — a longing for something absent.

steps.title: The three performing forces
steps.body:
The forces are **simple**, and that is worth saying in an answer: three lines only.

- **female voice**
- **acoustic guitar**
- **acoustic bass guitar**

An **acoustic bass guitar** is a larger version of the acoustic guitar with **four strings**, tuned **E, A, D, G** — the same tuning as the double bass and the electric bass. Spalding **sings and plays it herself**. There is no credit for a guitarist on the recording, and a second guitar part appears in the guitar solo, although in live performance one guitarist plays a simplified version.

**The voice.** It sits **low in the female range**, in the **chest register**, covering a **minor tenth** — an octave plus a minor third, from the E below middle C to the G above. The words are set **syllabically**: one note to each syllable. The line has many **leaps** and some complex rhythms — triplets, semiquavers and rests. Spalding keeps closely to the printed **pitches**, but varies the **rhythms and the tempo**, which is **rubato**.

**The bass does far more than hold the roots.** The opening is a **virtuosic bass solo** using **double stops**, wide leaps, rapid semiquaver passages, a **mordent** and a **harmonic**. During verse 1, before the guitar enters, the bass seems to play **two parts at once** — low bass notes alternating with higher chords, rather like a ragtime piano.

**The guitar** joins the accompaniment at **bar 23** and plays a virtuosic solo from **bar 55 to bar 88**. Accompanying, it mixes plucked chords with small melodic fragments that fill the long notes at the ends of vocal phrases, and at **bars 25 to 27** it seems to **imitate the vocal line**.

steps.title: Structure: two melodies, then both at once
steps.body:
The shape of this song is unusual and it is the thing to get right. There are **two melodies**, called **A** and **B**. They are heard **separately** first, and then **at the same time**.

That combination, at **bars 89 to 104**, is the structural point of the whole piece: the **bass plays melody A** while the **voice sings melody B**. Nothing new is introduced — the payoff is made from what you have already heard.

| Bars | Section | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 to 3 | Introduction | florid bass guitar solo |
| 4 to 19 | Verse 1 (A) | an eight-bar idea, repeated with a changed ending |
| 19 to 22 | Link | bass picks up the tempo into the bossa nova |
| 23 to 54 | Verse 2 (B) | a sixteen-bar idea, repeated and changed |
| 55 to 88 | Guitar solo | over the chords of verse 2 |
| 89 to 104 | Voice and bass duet | bass plays A, voice sings B |
| D.S. to end | Coda | second half of verse 2, the last line repeated, florid riffs under the last held note |

**Notice what this is not.** There is no chorus. Both verses are built the same way — **an idea stated, then repeated with a changed ending** — which is worth saying, because it is the same principle at two different lengths: eight bars in A, sixteen in B.

steps.title: Tonality and harmony: complex, but it never moves
steps.body:
**The key is B minor**, and this is the trap: despite harmony complicated enough to sound as though it must be going somewhere, **the music does not modulate at all**. It stays in B minor from start to finish.

Many bossa novas use **minor keys**, so B minor is typical of the style rather than exceptional.

**What makes the harmony sound complex** is the jazz influence, and it shows in four nameable ways:

- **Chord extensions** — extra thirds piled on top of the triad to give **sevenths, ninths, elevenths and thirteenths**. This is a hallmark of jazz harmony.
- **Unusual chord types** — a **diminished seventh** at bar 35, a **flattened fifth chord** at bar 44.
- **Chromatic chords**, containing notes outside B minor — **C sharp 7** at bar 31, and **C major and F major** at bars 27 and 28.
- **A descending chromatic bass**, moving down by semitone through bars 30 to 38.

**Underneath all of that, the roots are ordinary.** The movement of the chord roots is still based around chords **I, II, IV and V** — the same foundations as much simpler music. Saying that in an answer shows you can hear past the surface.

**Cadences** are not used as they would be in classical music, but the ends of sections still land somewhere definite: on **chord V** at bar 11, halfway through the verse, and on a conventional **perfect cadence, V to I**, at bars 52 to 53.

steps.title: The two melodies, compared
steps.body:
The two melodies are **opposites** in how they move, which makes each easy to follow when they are combined at the end.

**Verse 1 (A), bars 4 to 19** — an eight-bar idea (bars 4 to 11), repeated with a different ending (bars 12 to 19).

- Phrases are linked by a common **rising arpeggio** shape.
- The first or second note of each phrase **descends by a semitone or a tone**, making a long downward **sequence**.
- The line falls almost below the female range, to a **low E** at bar 11.
- It moves, unusually, **mostly by leaps** — thirds, and occasionally a seventh at bars 8 to 9.
- Every phrase spans a **seventh**, apart from the first, which spans a **minor sixth**.
- Bars 12 to 17 repeat bars 4 to 9, but developed by **rhythmic** change rather than melodic change.
- At bar 18 a **jazzy flattened fifth**, F natural, prepares the descent to the tonic.

**Verse 2 (B), bars 23 to 54** — a sixteen-bar idea, repeated with a different ending.

- In contrast to A, this melody is **almost entirely conjunct** — it moves by step.
- Bars 23 to 26 descend to the **leading note**, the raised seventh, A sharp here.
- Bars 27 to 30 answer with a rising and falling idea, itself related to the end of verse 1.
- Bars 31 to 34 are **in sequence** with bars 23 to 26, a **fourth higher**.
- Bars 34 to 35 repeat the **flattened fifth** idea from the end of verse 1, the second time a note lower in sequence.

**So: A leaps, B steps.** That single contrast is the most useful thing to remember, and it helps the ear tell the two lines apart when the bass plays A under the voice's B.

steps.title: Tempo, metre and the bossa nova rhythm
steps.body:
**The metre is 4/4 throughout**, apart from two bars. But from bar 19 onwards the music **sounds** as though it is moving in **two minims to a bar**, like 2/2, because of the change of speed.

**Three tempos, in order:**

1. **Bars 1 to 3** — very free. It is hard to hear a strong pulse at all.
2. **Verse 1** — slow, with a great deal of **rubato**, meaning freedom taken with the tempo.
3. **From bar 19** — the tempo **almost doubles** as the bass begins the bossa nova. A free tempo returns near the end, at bar 114.

**Here is the subtle point**, and it is a grade 8 to 9 one. The tempo doubles at bar 19 **and the note values double as well**. So the phrases of verse 2 *look* twice as long on the page as those of verse 1, but they are not: the two changes **cancel out**. The apparent increase in phrase length is **false**.

**The bossa nova rhythm itself** is a **dotted crotchet and quaver** pair. The bass plays close to this standard pattern from **bar 23**, still with some syncopation and quaver movement. In verse 1 it only occasionally touches the bossa nova pattern — at bars 6, 9, 10, 14 and 17.

**Vocal rhythms.** In verse 1 they are complex, with frequent **triplets** and rests separating the phrases, but never syncopated enough to lose the beat. In verse 2 the notes are longer but tend to **start off the beat**, sometimes a quaver early, and there are fewer triplets. From bar 89, where the two melodies combine, the verse 2 rhythms become **less syncopated**, perhaps so that they fit against verse 1 more easily.

steps.title: Texture: three kinds, and where each one is
steps.body:
This piece is useful for texture because it contains **three different textures**, each clearly located.

- **Monophonic** — a single line of music. The **introduction**, apart from a couple of double stops.
- **Homophonic** — tune and accompaniment. **Most** of the piece. But note that the bass part is sometimes melodic enough to count as a melody in its own right, which blurs the edge.
- **Polyphonic** — two or more separate melodic lines at once. **Bars 89 to 104**, where the two melodies of the piece are combined.

That last one matters twice over: it is both the **structural** climax and the **textural** one. If a question asks what is special about bars 89 to 104, either is a valid point, and giving both covers you.

**A word of caution about the introduction.** It is described as monophonic *apart from* the double stops — a double stop sounds two notes at once, so strictly the texture is not single-line there. Saying *essentially monophonic, with occasional double stops* is more accurate than either extreme, and accuracy of that kind is what a strong answer shows.

steps.title: Your turn: build the map yourself
steps.body:
**Part A.** From memory, write out the seven sections in order with their bar numbers.

**Part B.** Answer in one sentence each:

1. Who composed the music, who wrote the words, and who performs it here?
2. What key is the piece in, and how many times does it modulate?
3. What are the three performing forces?
4. What is the standard bossa nova rhythm?

**Part C.** Two harder ones:

5. Verse 2 has phrases that look twice as long as verse 1's. Explain why they are not.
6. Name the two traditions that bossa nova fuses, and give **one** feature in this piece that comes from each.

**Part D.** Write a paragraph on the texture of the piece, naming all three textures and locating each one.

For question 1, remember the set work is listed under the name of the **performer**.

steps.title: Going deeper: writing about a fusion
steps.body:
**Name the tradition, then the feature, then where it is.** A weak answer says the piece *mixes Brazilian music with jazz*. A strong one says **which** feature comes from **which** tradition and **where** it happens:

- **From Brazil**: the **bossa nova rhythm** — a dotted crotchet and quaver pair — which the bass plays from bar 23. Bossa nova itself grew out of **samba**.
- **From jazz**: the **chord extensions** — sevenths, ninths, elevenths and thirteenths — and chords like the diminished seventh at bar 35 and the flattened fifth at bar 44.
- **From both**: the **minor key**, typical of bossa nova, and the **improvisatory freedom** of the rubato and the guitar solo.

**Complexity is not modulation.** The harmony is extended and full of chromatic chords, and the piece still never leaves B minor. It is easy to hear the chromatic descent at bars 30 to 38 and write that it modulates. It does not. The chord **roots** stay around I, II, IV and V.

**The false lengthening at bar 19** is the single best detail to have ready. Tempo doubles, note values double, so the phrases only look longer. It shows you are reading the score and hearing the music, not one or the other.

**Use bars 89 to 104 for more than one thing.** It is the structural climax (the two melodies combined), the textural climax (the only polyphony), and it explains a rhythmic detail (the verse 2 rhythms become less syncopated, perhaps so they fit against verse 1). One passage, three points, in three different questions.

**A leaps, B steps.** If you remember one thing about the melodies, remember that. It is the contrast the whole piece is built on, and it keeps the two lines distinct when they are combined.

**For Section B**, which sets a set work against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, this piece pairs naturally with anything that sets a folk or traditional style against a Western harmonic language — which is also what *Release* does. Comparing what each **keeps** from its traditional source and what each **changes** is a more useful line than listing instruments.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Area of Study 4: Fusions.** The other set work is Afro Celt Sound System, *Release*.
- **Bossa nova** means *new trend*: Brazilian **samba** crossed with **jazz**.
- **Baden Powell** composed it, **Vinicius de Moraes** wrote the Portuguese words, **Esperanza Spalding** performs it.
- Written **1962**; on the album *Esperanza*, 2008.
- Forces: **female voice, acoustic guitar, acoustic bass guitar**. Spalding sings and plays the bass.
- The bass guitar has **four strings**, tuned **E, A, D, G**.
- The voice is **low, chest register**, spanning a **minor tenth**, set **syllabically**, with **rubato**.
- Opening bass solo uses **double stops, a mordent and a harmonic**.
- Structure: Introduction, Verse 1 (A), Link, Verse 2 (B), Guitar solo, **Voice and bass duet**, Coda.
- At **bars 89 to 104** the bass plays **A** while the voice sings **B**.
- Key: **B minor**, and the piece **never modulates**.
- Jazz harmony: **extensions** (7ths, 9ths, 11ths, 13ths), a **diminished seventh** at bar 35, a **flattened fifth** at bar 44, chromatic chords, a chromatic descending bass at bars 30 to 38.
- Chord roots still move around **I, II, IV and V**.
- **Melody A leaps; melody B steps.**
- Metre is **4/4** throughout apart from two bars, but sounds like 2/2 from bar 19.
- The tempo **almost doubles at bar 19** — and so do the note values, so the phrases only **look** longer.
- Bossa nova rhythm: a **dotted crotchet and quaver** pair, in the bass from bar 23.
- Textures: **monophonic** introduction, mostly **homophonic**, **polyphonic** at bars 89 to 104.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of Samba em Preludio, and explain why the passage at bars 89 to 104 can be called the climax of the piece.
questions.solution: The song falls into seven sections. It opens with a florid unaccompanied bass solo in bars 1 to 3, in a very free tempo. Verse 1, melody A, runs from bar 4 to bar 19 and consists of an eight-bar idea repeated with a changed ending. A short link at bars 19 to 22 lets the bass pick up the tempo, which almost doubles, and move into the bossa nova. Verse 2, melody B, runs from bar 23 to bar 54 and is a sixteen-bar idea, again repeated with a changed ending. The guitar then takes a virtuosic solo from bar 55 to bar 88, played over the chords of verse 2. At bars 89 to 104 the voice and bass form a duet, and finally the piece closes with a coda, after a D.S., made of the second half of verse 2 and repetitions of the last line, with florid guitar and bass riffs under the final held vocal note. The passage at bars 89 to 104 is the climax for three reasons. Structurally, the two melodies heard separately earlier are combined, with the bass playing melody A while the voice sings melody B, so the payoff is made entirely from material already heard rather than from anything new. Texturally, it is the only polyphonic passage in a piece that is otherwise essentially monophonic at the start and mostly homophonic thereafter. Rhythmically, the vocal rhythms of verse 2 become less syncopated here, which suggests the combination was prepared rather than improvised. The two melodies also contrast in motion, A mostly by leap and B almost entirely by step, so each stays clear against the other.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The seven sections.** Introduction (bars 1 to 3, a florid bass solo in free tempo); Verse 1, melody A (bars 4 to 19, an eight-bar idea repeated with a changed ending); Link (bars 19 to 22, the bass picks up the tempo, which almost doubles, into the bossa nova); Verse 2, melody B (bars 23 to 54, a sixteen-bar idea, repeated and changed); Guitar solo (bars 55 to 88, over the chords of verse 2); Voice and bass duet (bars 89 to 104); Coda (D.S. to the end).

**Why bars 89 to 104 are the climax — three reasons, and a strong answer gives more than one:**

- **Structural**: the bass plays melody **A** while the voice sings melody **B**. The two melodies heard separately are now heard together, so the climax is made from material already known.
- **Textural**: it is the **only polyphonic** passage. The introduction is essentially monophonic and the rest mostly homophonic.
- **Rhythmic**: the verse 2 vocal rhythms become **less syncopated** here, so the two lines fit together — which suggests the combination was planned (the guide says *perhaps* in order to fit).

**And why each line stays clear:** the two melodies are opposites. **A moves by leap, B by step**, so the ear can follow both.

questions.prompt: Explain how Samba em Preludio is a fusion, naming specific features and saying which tradition each one comes from.
questions.solution: Samba em Preludio is a bossa nova, and bossa nova is itself a fusion of Brazilian samba with American jazz. The Brazilian element is clearest in the rhythm. The standard bossa nova pattern is a dotted crotchet followed by a quaver, and the bass plays close to this from bar 23 onwards, though still with some syncopation and quaver movement. In verse 1 the bass touches the pattern only occasionally, at bars 6, 9, 10, 14 and 17, so the fusion is not evenly spread through the piece. The language is Portuguese and the lyrics use the word saudade, which has no direct English equivalent, and this too belongs to the Brazilian side. The jazz element is clearest in the harmony. There are frequent chord extensions, where extra thirds are piled on top of the triad to give sevenths, ninths, elevenths and thirteenths, and there are chords such as the diminished seventh at bar 35 and the flattened fifth at bar 44. Chromatic chords appear, including C sharp 7 at bar 31 and C and F major at bars 27 and 28, and there is a descending chromatic bass line through bars 30 to 38. The improvisatory freedom of the performance also belongs to jazz, both in the rubato of verse 1 and in the virtuosic guitar solo. Some features belong to both traditions. The minor key is typical of bossa nova, and beneath the complex surface the chord roots still move around chords I, II, IV and V, so the harmony remains essentially tonal despite the jazz colouring. Crucially, the piece never modulates.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The fusion is bossa nova**: Brazilian **samba** crossed with **jazz**.

**From Brazil:**

- The **bossa nova rhythm** — a **dotted crotchet and quaver** pair — played by the bass from **bar 23**. In verse 1 the bass touches it only occasionally, at bars 6, 9, 10, 14 and 17.
- The **Portuguese** lyrics, including *saudade*.

**From jazz:**

- **Chord extensions**: sevenths, ninths, elevenths and thirteenths piled on the triad.
- A **diminished seventh** at bar 35 and a **flattened fifth** at bar 44.
- **Chromatic chords**: C sharp 7 at bar 31, C and F major at bars 27 and 28, and a chromatic descending bass at bars 30 to 38.
- **Improvisatory freedom**: the rubato of verse 1, and the guitar solo.

**From both:** the **minor key**, typical of bossa nova.

**And the point about tonality:** underneath all of it the chord roots still move around **I, II, IV and V**, and the piece **never modulates**. Complex surface, ordinary foundations.

questions.prompt: Compare the use of the bass guitar in this piece with the way a bass part usually works in popular music.
questions.solution: In most popular music the bass has a supporting role. It plays the root of each chord, locks in with the drums to define the beat, and rarely carries melodic interest of its own. In Samba em Preludio the bass does all of these things at times but also does considerably more, and Esperanza Spalding plays it while singing. The piece opens with a completely unaccompanied bass solo in bars 1 to 3, which is florid and virtuosic and uses double stops, wide leaps, rapid semiquaver passages, a mordent and a harmonic. These are techniques associated with a solo instrument rather than an accompanying one, and the tempo here is so free that it is difficult to hear a pulse at all, which is the opposite of the timekeeping role a bass usually has. During verse 1, before the acoustic guitar enters, the bass appears to play two parts at once, with low bass notes alternating with higher chords rather like a ragtime piano, so it supplies both bass line and harmony. Its rhythms in verse 1 are actually more syncopated than the vocal line, which reverses the usual relationship in which the voice is free and the bass is steady. From bar 23 the bass does take up a more conventional role, playing close to the standard bossa nova rhythm of a dotted crotchet and quaver pair. The most striking departure comes at bars 89 to 104, where the bass plays melody A while the voice sings melody B. Here the bass is not accompanying at all but carrying one of the two themes of the piece, producing the only polyphonic texture in the song.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The usual role.** In most popular music the bass plays the **root** of each chord, locks in with the drums, and carries little melodic interest.

**What it does here instead:**

- **Opens the piece alone** — a florid, virtuosic solo in bars 1 to 3, using **double stops, wide leaps, rapid semiquavers, a mordent and a harmonic**. These belong to a solo instrument, not an accompanying one, and the tempo is so free that there is barely a pulse — the opposite of a timekeeping role.
- **Plays two parts at once** in verse 1, with low bass notes alternating with higher chords, **like a ragtime piano**, so it supplies both bass and harmony.
- **Is more syncopated than the voice** in verse 1, reversing the usual relationship.
- **Takes a conventional role from bar 23**, playing close to the standard bossa nova rhythm.
- **Carries a melody** at **bars 89 to 104**, playing **A** against the voice's **B** — producing the piece's only polyphonic texture.

**And throughout, Spalding is singing at the same time**, which is worth a sentence in itself.

examTechnique.body:
Name Baden Powell as the composer and Vinicius de Moraes as the lyricist, and describe Esperanza Spalding as the performer.

Say that the piece is in B minor and never modulates, however complex the harmony sounds.

When asked about the fusion, name the tradition, the feature and where it happens, rather than saying the piece mixes Brazilian music with jazz.

Use bar numbers rather than describing where something happens by how far into the track it is.

For a question on bars 89 to 104, give the structural point and the textural point, since both are valid.

Remember that melody A moves by leap and melody B by step.

If a question asks about phrase lengths in verse 2, explain that the tempo and the note values both double.
examinerErrors: Naming Esperanza Spalding as the composer.
Saying the piece modulates because the harmony is chromatic.
Calling the bossa nova rhythm a jazz feature; it comes from samba.
Describing verse 2 as having longer phrases than verse 1.
Saying the metre changes at bar 19; only the tempo does.
Calling the whole piece homophonic and missing the polyphony at bars 89 to 104.
Describing the introduction as simply monophonic, when double stops sound two notes.
Writing about the fusion in general terms without naming a feature or a bar.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never confuses the performer with the composer, and it knows why the confusion arises. It hears past the surface of the harmony: extensions, chromatic chords and a chromatic bass, over roots that still move around I, II, IV and V, in a piece that never changes key. It can say which feature comes from Brazil and which from jazz, and point to a bar for each. It treats bars 89 to 104 as the centre of the piece and gives more than one reason why. And it knows the small, telling detail — that the doubling of tempo at bar 19 is matched by a doubling of note values, so the phrases only look longer on the page.
